newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds lawyer says smoker made choice.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds lawyer says smoker made choice.

text.p: In the second half of his closing argument at a wrongful death trial, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co attorney Paul Crist said smoking was a lifestyle choice that Jean Connor made despite "widespread, unprecedented" public knowledge about the health risks.
Crist told the six-member jury hearing a lawsuit filed by Connor's family that polls from the 1960s indicated more than 90 percent of the public was aware of the risks.
"The evidence is absolutely overwhelming that there was vast, widespread, unprecedented knowledge in the public domain about the health risks of smoking," he said.

In a closing address lasting nearly two and a half hours, Crist told the jury that while science had not been able to determine definitively that smoking caused cancer and other diseases, reputable authorities including the U.S. Surgeon General had "exercised judgment" that smoking causes cancer.
"That judgment may be right in my client's opinion," he said.
Crist argued that cigarette smoking differed from the use of other substances to which people were commonly believed to become addicted and could not be compared to alcohol and drugs.
"Cigarette smoking is not intoxicating. People don't get drunk because they smoke," he said. "When they stop smoking ... they don't have life-threatening withdrawal."
"Smokers don't mug little old ladies. They don't sell their children. They don't prostitute themselves," he said.
He hammered on the central theme of his closing argument -- that Connor knew there were health risks associated with smoking but did it anyway.

Crist said Connor, a three-pack-a-day smoker, would have had up to 591,000 exposures to warning labels on cigarette packages in the 27 years she smoked after the labels were put on cigarette packages, in addition to mass media coverage of the potential health risks.

He said the warning on cigarette packages was so widely known that it had become part of the popular culture and was used by people to describe other risks, such as "parenting can be hazardous to your health."
He told jurors that the plaintiffs had cast a "shadow" over the case by not having an autopsy done on Connor to determine where her cancer started.

Crist hailed American cigarette makers and particularly Reynolds as having "revolutionized cigarette design" with reductions in tar and nicotine, different filter materials and additives and new types of cigarette papers.
"The major advances have come out of this country and particularly this company. Good old American ingenuity at its best," he said.
The plaintiffs were to make a short rebuttal before Judge Bernard Nachman instructed the jury.
